The lesson on prior knowledge asked one question of one spring: does it help
an agent to be told the form of the law? One system is one data point. A
**benchmark** asks the same question of several systems, under rules fixed
before any run, so that its results can be read side by side and checked by
someone else.

This lesson builds a small one. Three simulated systems from the mechanics
course hide a parameter: a projectile in a world of unknown gravity, a mass
on a spring of unknown stiffness, and a force that falls with an unknown
power of the distance. On each, the same language model is asked to find the
law under three conditions of prior knowledge, **full**, **partial**, and
**none**, as in the lesson on prior knowledge. That makes a grid of
`{python} result["runs"]` runs. Four of them are the frozen runs of the
earlier lessons, read from their pages; the other five were recorded for this
one under the same protocols.

The build replays every run, scores it again on settings the agent could not
probe, and asks two further questions. Did the readings each run collected
support the answer, whatever the agent concluded? And of the comparisons a
reader might draw from the grid, which does the design actually allow?

## Assumptions

1. **One protocol per system.** On each system the model, the system prompt,
   the tools and their bounds, the budget of `{python} result["budget"]`
   probes, the step limit, the seed, the tolerance, and the held-out settings
   belong to one protocol object (the Discovery evaluation protocol). Only
   the task text differs between the conditions, and a cell below checks it.
2. **The three protocols share their numbers, not their systems.** The budget,
   the step limit, the seed, and the tolerance are the same on every system.
   The systems, their hidden values, and their held-out settings are not, so
   a result on one system says nothing directly about another.
3. **The systems are simulated, and their noise is repeatable.** Each reading
   has Gaussian noise that depends on the setting and the seed only: probing
   the same setting twice gives the same reading. A replay is therefore exact,
   and an agent that repeats a probe learns nothing new.
4. **One run per cell.** Each system and condition was run once, by a Claude
   model in a Claude Code session, as described under "The runs".
5. **The hidden values are the judge's.** The page never prints them, and the
   comparability check below names what differs between two protocols, never
   its value.

## A benchmark as a grid {#explanation}

A benchmark of discovery has three parts, and each must be fixed before the
first run:

- **The tasks**: here three systems, each a black box with controls, a noisy
  reading, and a hidden law of known form.
- **The conditions**: here what the agent is told. Within a system, only this
  may change from run to run.
- **The judge**: the held-out settings, outside the range the agent may probe,
  and the error that counts as recovering the law. The score of a claim is the
  root-mean-square error of its predictions there, relative to the size of the
  reading, and the law is recovered when that error is at most
  `{python} result["tolerance"]`.

A comparison read from the grid is meaningful only when everything but the
thing compared is equal. Within a column (one system) the conditions can be
compared, because the protocol is shared. Across columns they cannot be
compared directly: a projectile and a spring differ in the law, the hidden
value, the held-out settings, and how hard the noise makes them. Between an
agent and a method without one, the comparison is meaningful when both had
the same system and the same number of probes allowed. The build does not
leave this to the reader: `comparable` reads the protocols of two scored
entries and lists what differs.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.discovery.benchmark import comparable

excerpt(comparable)
```

In every run the agent may call `measure` at most `{python} result["budget"]`
times and `submit` once, in at most `{python} result["max-steps"]` messages of
at most `{python} result["max-calls"]` tool calls each; calls beyond that
number in one message are refused unrun and cost no probe.

## Code

Every run is replayed from its frozen trace with the tools of its run, and
scored again by executing its tool calls on a fresh copy of its system. The
replay and the score are those of the Discovery evaluation protocol.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.discovery.benchmark import fit_readings, replay_cell

excerpt(replay_cell)
```

What a run's readings support is answered apart from what its agent
concluded, by fitting the law's family to exactly the readings the agent saw:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(fit_readings)
```

## Worked examples

### The runs

The five new runs were recorded on the same day by the same Claude model
working in a Claude Code session, each as a fresh sub-agent that was given the
system prompt, its task, the tool descriptions, and an instruction to answer in
the harness's format and to use no tool of its own. It chose every call after
reading the readings the harness computed; none knew of the others. The four
runs of the earlier lessons were recorded the same way, by the same model, on
an earlier date.

mixes systems whose held-out errors mean different things.

### Run the agents yourself

This needs your own key and costs a few cents per run. The build does not run
it, so the commands are marked.

::: {.not-verified}
```bash
uv sync --locked --no-dev --extra openai
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."
cd site/lessons/agents-llm/12-interactive-discovery-benchmarks
uv run --locked --no-dev --extra openai python -m pbc.discovery.benchmark projectile-full projectile-partial projectile-none central-full central-none
```
:::

With `--record` the command writes the fixture of each run in the current
directory. A benchmark worth stating runs every cell many times, on several
seeds and several hidden values; it runs outside the build, and its results
would be marked "not verified" here.

## Limits {#limits}

- **One run per cell cannot rank the conditions.** Full recovered on all three
  systems and the other conditions on two; with one run each, a second round
  could reverse that.
- **Round hidden values flatter the agents.** On the projectile and the
  central force the hidden values are round numbers, and agents that rounded
  their estimates landed on them exactly. A benchmark should draw its hidden
  values so that rounding gains nothing, and should vary them (held-out
  worlds); this one fixed one value per system before the runs and kept it.
- **The systems are easy.** Each hides one or two parameters of a law whose
  form the tools reveal. The conditions leak through the tools: the claim's
  parameters are named and described in every condition.
- **The noise repeats.** A repeated probe returns the same reading. That makes
  the replay exact, and it means repetition cannot average noise away; an
  agent must vary its settings.
- **The recordings are not API runs.** They are Claude Code sessions, told by
  the session to answer in the harness's format and to use no tool of their
  own. A first round of recordings for this lesson was refused by the model
  provider's safeguards because of the wording of that instruction, and one
  retry answered with a summary instead of a message; both were discarded
  before any run was kept. The sessions reported no token count or price.
- **Simulated, not measured.** Nothing here is a reading of a real system.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
On the central force, the full, partial, and none runs all recovered the law,
and the full runs on the projectile and on the spring both recovered it. Which
statement does this benchmark support?

::: {.choices}
::: {.choice}
The projectile is as easy for the agent as the spring, because both full runs
recovered.

::: {.feedback}
The two systems have different laws, hidden values, and held-out settings.
The comparability check says the comparison is not meaningful, and one run
each could not support it anyway.
:::
:::

::: {.choice correct="true"}
On each system, under one protocol, these runs recovered the law in the
cells the table shows; the readings of every run supported a recovery; and
nothing here ranks the conditions or the systems.

::: {.feedback}
Right. The benchmark supports statements about its runs and its protocols;
ranking needs many runs per cell.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
Prior knowledge does not matter on the central force, because every condition
recovered the law.

::: {.feedback}
Three runs that all succeed are consistent with prior knowledge helping a
little, a lot, or not at all; the round hidden values also made the task
easy to hit exactly.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.solution}
The supported statement is the narrow one: each claim's score on its
system's held-out settings, the fit to each run's readings, and which
comparisons the protocols allow. The other two compare across systems or
read an effect into one run per cell.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
Full recovered on three systems of three, partial and none on two of three.
How likely is a difference at least this large if the condition made no
difference at all? Use Fisher's exact test on the two-by-two table of
recovered and not recovered.

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.chance)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("ev2-chance")
```

A difference of one recovery in three runs is what chance gives most of the
time: the test cannot tell it from no effect. To detect even a large effect
the benchmark needs many runs per cell, which is why a full benchmark runs
outside the build.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
The run of the lesson on a modified force law uses the same environment class, tools, budget,
and tolerance as the central-force column. Why does the check still refuse
to compare it with the partial run of that column, and what would have to
change for the comparison to be meaningful?

::: {.solution}
The check reads the protocols: the hidden worlds differ, so a recovery in
one is a different task from a recovery in the other, even though nothing in
the transcripts shows it. To compare them, both runs would have to be scored
under one protocol, with the same hidden world and held-out settings; or the
benchmark would have to draw the hidden worlds from one stated distribution
and compare recovery rates over many worlds, not two runs.
:::
:::
